newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rexrodt stands by plan to cut solidarity tax.
newsitem.headline: Rexrodt stands by plan to cut solidarity tax.

text.p: Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Monday the government stands by its plan to cut the solidarity tax surcharge in January 1998, overruling weekend comments by the new commissioner for east German affairs.

Rexrodt, whose Free Democratic Party is fundamentally in favour of lower taxes, said in a radio interview that discussion was closed on the two percentage point cut in the solidarity tax to 5.5 percent, which is a centrepiece of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's planned tax reform.

Rexrodt was responding to remarks made by Rudi Geil, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's newly appointed commissioner for east German affairs, who said the planned cut in the solidarity tax would send the wrong signal, as transfers to the east would remain high for years to come.
Rexrodt agreed subsidies for the formerly communist eastern states would remain at a high level in 1998, supported by the solidarity tax, and that he would unveil a detailed proposal in a few days.

Rexrodt said he was open to discussion of a rise in the value-added tax, but only to finance a tax reform that resulted in a net reduction in citizens' tax burden, not to finance the development of east Germany.
